transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well... hi. Thank you for fitting me in. I, um... I honestly wasn't sure where to start, or if I even needed to be here, but I guess I'm here because of work. It's just taking over everything. 

I've been a quality inspector for years, right? Testing, sorting, weighing samples, making sure everything is strictly up to code. I have my associate's degree, I know my job inside and out, and I've always taken a lot of pride in being accurate. But lately... well, ever since corporate brought in this new operations manager, it's just been an absolute nightmare. He just—he started picking apart the inspection procedures I’ve used for years. Just completely micromanaging and dismantling how I do things, even though my track record is spotless and those procedures have always worked perfectly fine. 

And the thing is, because of all this, I just can’t seem to leave work at work anymore. I used to be so good at that! I'd clock out, leave the samples and the clipboards behind, and just go home and be normal. But now... I drive home and I am just completely wound up. My shoulders are practically up to my ears by the time I pull into the driveway. I walk in the door, and my poor husband, he just tries to ask about my day or ask what's for dinner, and I just snap at him. Just bite his head right off for no reason. 

And then I feel terrible about it, so I go to bed, but I can't even rest. I just lie awake for hours, staring at the ceiling, replaying every single meeting we had that day, over and over in my head. I think about what this manager said, how he looked at my daily reports, what I should have said back to him... And then the worst part—the absolute worst part—is that the next day, I go in exhausted, and I start second-guessing myself on the floor. I'm standing there second-guessing routine quality calls that I used to make without any trouble at all. I just stand there staring at the scales, doubting my own eyes and my own judgment. It's just... it's exhausting, and I just don't know how to turn my brain off anymore.
Outside of work and interactions with your manager, do you find yourself feeling anxious or stressed in other areas of your life, like with family, friends, or while doing routine tasks?

Well, yes, definitely at home. Like I mentioned a minute ago about snapping at my husband, it’s... it's really escalating. We are just arguing so much more than we ever have. Usually, he’s a very patient man, but I am just so constantly on edge now. I walk in the door and if he’s left his shoes in the hallway, or if he asks a simple, innocent question about whether I paid the water bill, I just explode. We bicker about the absolute smallest things, and it just breaks my heart because it’s not him, it’s me. 

And because of all that tension, I’m just not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to. We used to have this whole system, you know? We’d cook dinner together—I’d chop the vegetables, he’d handle the stove, we’d sit down and watch Jeopardy. It was nice. It was predictable. But now? Now I can’t even bring myself to figure out what to make for dinner, let alone actually cook it. I just come home, drop my bag, and sit on the couch in my work clothes for an hour, just staring into space. The mail is piling up on the counter, the laundry is sitting in baskets... I just don't have the energy for any of it anymore.

And honestly, even though you asked about outside of work, it’s... it’s bleeding back into my actual job performance, too, which just makes the stress even worse. My work record has actually taken a hit recently. Me! I have never had a blemish on my record, but lately, I’ve actually missed internal deadlines for my inspection reports. I get so paralyzed by all his micromanaging that I just can't finish them on time. And I’ve even started pulling back from meetings I’m fully expected to attend. I just... I find myself organizing the sample closet or hiding out in the breakroom right when the weekly operations meeting is starting, just to avoid sitting at that conference table with him. I know I'm supposed to be there, but I just can't face it. So, yes, to answer your question, it feels like everything—my marriage, my house, my actual job performance—is just completely slipping through my fingers.
Do you find that you worry constantly about a wide range of things, even when there isn't a clear reason for concern?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. It's really just... it's just this one thing, you know? It's not like I'm sitting around worrying about the economy, or my health, or, I don't know, getting into a car accident or something. I've never been a worrier. Never. My sister, now, she's a worrier. She worries if it rains, she worries if it doesn't rain. But me? I've always been the practical one. The grounded one. If there's a problem, I fix it. That's why I'm so good at my job! Or... why I used to be. 

But this... this situation at work with this new manager, it's just so specific to him and what he's doing to my department. It's like a dark cloud that just hangs over my head, but it's got his name written all over it. I'm not waking up in a panic about random things, I'm waking up in a panic about my daily inspection logs and whether he's going to scrutinize the calibration on my scales. So, no, I wouldn't say my mind is just spinning out of control about everything in the world. It's just spinning out of control about *this*. And I think that's what makes it so incredibly frustrating! Because I can point right at the problem, right at his office door, but I can't seem to stop it from ruining my evenings and making me snap at my husband. If he would just let me do my job the way I've done it for the last fifteen years, I honestly believe all of this—the sleeplessness, the arguing, the lack of energy—would just go away. It's just him. It's just this one, giant, unavoidable problem.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like cooking with your husband or watching Jeopardy?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad. Not like, crying or feeling down in the dumps, you know? It's not a sadness thing. And it's not that I've lost interest in Jeopardy! I mean, I love Jeopardy. We've watched it every single weeknight for, gosh, it has to be over a decade now. Ken Jennings is doing a wonderful job hosting, by the way, though I obviously still miss Alex. But anyway, I still genuinely *want* to watch it, and I still *want* to cook those nice meals with my husband. I really do. 

It's just... I just don't have the bandwidth for it right now. It's not that I don't care about those things anymore, it's just that by the time I get home, my brain is so completely fried from dealing with all the new protocols and the constant hovering from that manager, I just can't focus on the TV screen. I'll sit there on the couch while the show is on, and my husband will be shouting out the answers—he's very good at the history categories, by the way, terrible at pop culture, but great at history—and I'll suddenly realize I haven't heard a single clue. Not one! Because I'm too busy sitting there agonizing over whether I signed off on the right batch numbers at 3:00 PM, or if the manager is going to pull my logs first thing in the morning. 

So, no, it's definitely not sadness, and it's not losing interest in my life. It's just... this absolute, total depletion of my energy. If I had my way, if things were just back to normal at the plant and he would just leave my department alone, I'd be right back at that stove chopping onions and guessing the Daily Doubles without a second thought. I just can't seem to get my head clear enough to actually be present and enjoy those things right now.
When you're at work and dealing with the manager or thinking about the changes he's made, do you notice any physical reactions like a racing heart, sweating, or feeling shaky?

Well, let me think about that... no, not really. I mean, you see that kind of thing on TV, don't you? Someone gets stressed and suddenly they're sweating buckets or their hands are trembling like a leaf. But honestly, I don't have anything like that. My heart isn't pounding out of my chest when he walks into the room. It's more of a... well, a mental clamping down, if that makes sense. 

Like just yesterday, for instance. He came down to the sorting floor right when I was finishing up my morning calibrations. We have these highly sensitive industrial scales, and they have to be calibrated first thing, every single shift, without fail. I've been doing it exactly the same way for fifteen years. Anyway, he comes strolling over, and I'm holding my clipboard, and my hands are perfectly steady. I'm not shaking at all. And I'm certainly not sweating—it's strictly climate-controlled in the testing area anyway because of the moisture sensitivity of the samples, so it's always quite cool in there. But inside? Inside I'm just so incredibly aggravated. 

It's not a panic attack or anything physical like that. I've actually seen someone have one of those—my cousin Brenda had one at a Fourth of July barbecue a few years back, thought she was having a full-blown heart attack. Sweating, shaking, gasping for air, the whole nine yards. We actually had to call an ambulance for her, it was quite the ordeal. But for me, with this manager? No, it's nothing like what Brenda went through. My blood pressure is usually perfectly fine at my yearly checkups, too. So no, my heart doesn't race. It's just my brain that won't stop. I can stand there looking perfectly calm, holding my pen completely steady, while he talks down to me about how to double-check a sample weight I’ve already verified three times. Physically, I'm not having those kinds of reactions. It's just the mental toll of it all that's wearing me down to the bone.
Do you find yourself actively avoiding certain situations at work—like specific tasks, areas of the plant, or interactions with your manager—because of the stress or discomfort it causes you?

Well, I suppose... yes, if I’m being completely honest with myself, I am. And I hate to admit it because I’ve always been the kind of person who tackles a problem head-on. But lately? I find myself finding reasons to just... not be where he is. 

Like, we have these weekly quality assurance syncs. They’re every Wednesday morning, usually in Conference Room B, and I’m expected to attend them. I used to be the first one in there, clipboard ready, bringing the updated spreadsheets for the whole sorting floor. But now... I find myself making excuses. I’ll tell the shift supervisor that I’m right in the middle of a complex batch check, or that the industrial scales need a secondary calibration, just so I can pull back from those meetings and avoid sitting across a table from him while he nitpicks every little thing. 

But the problem with hiding out like that is that it’s starting to really catch up with me. Because I’m pulling back from those meetings, I’m missing the updates on the new testing protocols, which means—and it just makes my stomach tie in knots to even say this out loud—I’ve actually missed some internal deadlines recently. My work record has taken a hit. After fifteen years! Fifteen years of spotless performance reviews, always exceeding expectations, and now my record is taking a hit because I’m so busy trying to dodge this man that I’m falling behind on my actual deliverables. It’s humiliating, frankly. I’m just trying to protect my peace of mind, but it’s completely backfiring on me.

And the worst part is, it doesn't even stay at the plant. It follows me right through my front door. Because I spend all day navigating this minefield, trying to avoid him and then stressing over the deadlines I missed because I was avoiding him, by the time I get home, my husband and I are just arguing more. We never used to bicker like this! But he’ll ask a simple question, like if I remembered to take the chicken out of the freezer, and I’ll just bite his head off. I’m so on edge that I’m just not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to. Like I said before about the dinners and the television... all of that structure we used to have, the things that made our house feel like a home, it's just falling apart. I’m not doing my part in the evenings because I’m too busy being angry about what happened at work, or what I had to avoid doing at work just to survive the shift. It’s just a giant mess.
Do you ever feel like you're worrying so much that it's hard to control, even about things that haven't happened yet or might not happen at all?

Oh, you mean like... like borrowing trouble? Worrying about things out of the blue that might never happen? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I've never been a 'what if' kind of person. My sister, now she's a worrier. She'll watch the evening news and suddenly she's convinced her basement is going to flood even though she lives at the top of a hill, or she'll fret for weeks about whether her car is going to break down just because it made a funny noise once. But me? No, I don't sit around spinning my wheels over imaginary scenarios. I really don't.

The things I'm agonizing over—they are happening. Very much so. Right there on the sorting floor. When I'm sitting on the couch completely zoning out while Ken Jennings is reading the Jeopardy clues, I'm not worrying about some hypothetical future disaster. I'm replaying the exact, real conversation I had with that manager at 2:15 PM about the moisture sensitivity protocols. I'm worrying about the actual, literal deadlines I just told you I missed because I skipped that Wednesday sync in Conference Room B. It's all very concrete. It's just... it's the reality of my day-to-day that's so overwhelming, not my imagination running wild. 

I mean, if he wasn't there, physically standing over my shoulder questioning my calibration logs, I wouldn't be worrying about a single thing! I'd be perfectly fine, just like I was for the last fifteen years. So it's definitely not some uncontrollable worry about things that don't exist or haven't happened. It's just him, and those new protocols, and the very real mess it's making of my flawless work record. That's what I can't stop thinking about. Nothing else.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or stressed in public places or during routine activities outside of work and home, like grocery shopping, driving, or running errands?

Oh, heavens no. Out in public? No, not at all. Actually, running errands is about the only time I feel like myself lately. 

Take the grocery store, for example. I go to the Kroger over on Elm Street every Sunday morning at 8:00 AM sharp. Have for years. And I'm perfectly fine. I actually find it quite relaxing, to be honest. Pushing the cart down the aisles, picking out the produce... I always inspect the apples and tomatoes myself, you know, old habits from being a quality inspector for so long. You look for the bruising, the color consistency, the firmness. But it doesn't stress me out! It's soothing. It's a process I control. Nobody is standing over my shoulder with a clipboard telling me I'm picking the wrong Fuji apple or asking me to document why I chose this carton of eggs over that one. 

And driving? Driving is an absolute breeze. I actually take the long way home sometimes just to decompress before I have to face the music at the house. I've always been a very logical person—I got my associate's degree in applied sciences, so I like things that make sense—and driving is just a logical process. Stop at the red, go at the green, use your blinker. There are clear, established rules on the road, unlike at the plant right now where the rules seem to change depending on what side of the bed this new manager wakes up on. 

So no, running errands or being out in public doesn't bother me one bit. I don't get panicky in crowds or anything like that. I can go to the post office, the bank, the dry cleaners—I just dropped off my husband's winter coat on Tuesday, actually, the heavy wool one that needs the special chemical treatment—and I'm as calm as a cucumber through all of it. The only time my stomach starts to turn is when I have to pull my car into that employee parking lot at the testing facility. But out in the real world, doing my normal day-to-day shopping? I'm completely fine.
Do you ever feel like you have no energy, even when you haven’t been stressed or busy?

Oh, no, definitely not. If I don't have anything stressing me out, I have more energy than I know what to do with! I am not a lethargic person by nature. I mean, I’ve been standing on my feet on a concrete sorting floor for fifteen years, so physically, I’m built for endurance. 

If you take away the stress of that plant and that new manager, I am a powerhouse. Just last weekend, for example, when I managed to actually put work out of my mind for a few hours on Saturday morning, I woke up at 6:00 AM without an alarm, completely ready to go. I decided right then and there to deep clean the entire kitchen. And I mean really deep clean, not just wiping down the counters. I actually pulled the refrigerator out from the wall—which is not an easy task, let me tell you, it’s one of those heavy double-door models we bought back in 2018 during a Memorial Day sale—and I got back there and vacuumed the condenser coils. Dust just accumulates there so quickly, and if you don't maintain it, the compressor has to work twice as hard. It's just simple thermodynamics, really. 

After that, I completely reorganized the pantry. I pulled every single can and box out, wiped down the shelving paper, and put it all back sorted by expiration date, which took a good three hours because my husband just shoves things wherever there's an empty space when he unloads the groceries. 

So, no, my body has plenty of energy. My mother always used to say I was like a wind-up toy that never quite wound down. The only time I ever feel like I can't move, or when I'm just sitting there staring blankly at the television like I mentioned before, is when the stress from work is just crushing me. It’s the mental exhaustion of dealing with him and those new protocols that drains my physical battery. If I'm having a good, quiet day with no drama? I could run circles around people half my age.
Do you ever feel so overwhelmed by thoughts about work that you have trouble functioning normally in other parts of your life, like at home or during activities you used to handle easily?

Oh, absolutely. That’s... well, that’s the crux of the whole problem right there. It really is. Like I mentioned earlier about missing that Wednesday sync in Conference Room B? That wasn't just a one-off thing, unfortunately. My work record—which, like I told you, has been absolutely flawless for fifteen years, not a single reprimand—has really taken a hit lately. I’ve been missing internal deadlines left and right, and I’ve actually been pulling back from several meetings I’m fully expected to attend. I just... I can't face going into those rooms and having him question my methods in front of the junior sorters, so I just find an excuse to avoid it altogether, which is so unlike me. I’m a senior inspector, I belong in those meetings! 

And then I bring all that mess home with me, and it’s completely disrupting everything there, too. My husband and I are arguing so much more than we ever have in our entire marriage. Usually, we are like clockwork. I get home at 5:15, we have dinner, and then we have our usual evening routine—we watch the 6:30 local broadcast, then Jeopardy, and while that's on I normally prep my lunch for the next day. I like to portion out our leftovers into my glass Tupperware, you know, the ones with the snap-on silicone lids so they don't leak in my work tote. 

But lately? I'm just not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to at all. I walk in the door, I drop my bag, and I just sit there zoning out. I don't prep my lunch, I don't tidy up the living room. And if my husband asks me a simple question, like if I remembered to pick up the mail or what we should thaw out for dinner, I just snap at him. We end up bickering over the absolute silliest things because my mind is still stuck back on the sorting floor agonizing over my logs. He'll be trying to tell me about his day, and I'm a million miles away, just completely consumed by what happened at work. So yes, it's definitely spilling over and making a mess of everything else.
Do you find that your thoughts about work keep coming back to your mind throughout the day, even when you're trying to focus on something else?

Oh, constantly. It’s like a tape loop playing in my head that I just can’t find the stop button for. And honestly, doctor, that’s exactly why I’m here talking to you today. Because ever since this new operations manager started—the one who just insists on picking apart the inspection procedures I’ve used perfectly well for fifteen years—I just can’t seem to leave work at work. 

I try, I really do. But I come home so incredibly wound up. Like I was saying about snapping at my husband... that's exactly where it comes from. I'll be sitting there on the couch, supposedly relaxing, but in my mind, I'm right back on the sorting floor defending my logs. And it doesn't stop when I go to bed, either. I will lie awake for hours just staring at the ceiling fan—we have one of those Hunter fans with the dark mahogany blades in the bedroom—and I just lay there replaying those meetings over and over again. I'll analyze every little thing he said, his tone of voice, what I should have said back to him... 

And the absolute worst part is how it affects me the next day. Because my mind has been spinning all night, I go in, and I actually find myself second-guessing routine quality calls. Me! I'm a senior inspector, and I'm second-guessing standard defect checks that I used to make without any trouble at all, just pure muscle memory. I used to clear a batch in ten minutes, but now I stand there holding a piece, terrified I'm going to make a call he's going to use to write me up. So yes, the thoughts just never, ever stop, no matter what I'm trying to focus on.
Do you ever feel like your thoughts about work are completely out of your control, even when you’re actively trying to stop thinking about them?

Well, I don't know if I'd say they are *completely* out of my control. That makes it sound like I'm losing my mind or something, and I am definitely not doing that. I can still steer my own brain, it just takes a lot of effort right now. 

If I'm doing something that demands my absolute, undivided attention, I can push work out of my head. Like, just this past Sunday afternoon, my husband was trying to fix the carburetor on his riding mower. It’s a John Deere, we bought it secondhand about five years ago, and it's been making this awful sputtering noise whenever you engage the blades. Anyway, he has these thick fingers and he just couldn't get this tiny little retaining clip back onto the fuel line. He was getting so frustrated, his face was turning bright red, and it was already sweltering in the garage. 

So I went out there to help him, and I had to use my needle-nose pliers—the ones with the blue rubber grips that I usually keep in my craft drawer for jewelry making—and I had to get right in there at this very specific, awkward angle to snap it back into place. For those twenty minutes or so, I was so focused on not dropping that tiny little metal clip into the engine casing that I didn't think about the new operations manager or my inspection logs once. Not a single time. 

So I *can* stop thinking about work, and I can control it. It's just that... well, the second I washed the grease off my hands with the GoJo soap and sat back down in the living room with my iced tea, the worries just slipped right back in through the side door. The moment my mind isn't actively occupied by a complex task, the tape loop starts up again. But no, I wouldn't say I'm completely helpless to my own thoughts. I just have to work much, much harder to keep them at bay than I ever used to.
Have you noticed any days where you feel down or low, even when things at work are going relatively okay?

Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if things at work are actually going okay, then I feel completely fine. I'm not walking around feeling depressed or low for no reason, I promise you that. 

Like, take last Thursday for example. The new operations manager was actually out of the building for the entire day. He had some sort of regional compliance seminar down in Peoria, I think it was—one of those all-day things they hold in the conference center at the Marriott down there. Anyway, because he wasn't there pacing the floor, I went in and it was just exactly like the old days. I grabbed my clipboard, I checked the calibration on our digital scales—we use these highly sensitive Mettler Toledo scales on the line that have to be zeroed out perfectly every single morning before we can even begin—and I just went right to work. 

And doctor, I felt completely like myself. I cleared four pallets of components before my lunch break, I didn't second-guess a single defect call, and I was even humming along to the classic rock station they play over the warehouse speakers. I felt light. I wasn't down or sad whatsoever. And when I came home that evening, I actually had energy. I didn't just drop my bag and zone out on the couch like I've been doing. I actually made a proper dinner from scratch—I made my husband's favorite, chicken piccata with the capers and a nice side of angel hair pasta—and we had a lovely, normal evening together without a single argument. 

So, no, if the pressure at work isn't there and things are running the way they're supposed to, my mood is absolutely fine. I'm a very positive person by nature! It's really only when I'm dealing with him breathing down my neck and questioning my logs that I get so wound up and miserable. If work is okay, I'm okay.

Has the way you're feeling about work affected your ability to function in any other important areas of your life, like your relationship with your husband or your ability to manage daily responsibilities at home?

Well, yes, it absolutely has, and that's the part that really scares me, to be perfectly honest with you. Because I have always been someone who takes pride in keeping everything running smoothly, both at the warehouse and at home. 

But lately... well, my work record has actually taken a real hit, which is just devastating to me because I have had a spotless file for fifteen years. Not a single disciplinary mark. But because I'm so paralyzed by this new manager and double-checking everything I do, I’ve actually started missing our internal deadlines. We have these end-of-week quality assurance summaries that absolutely have to be submitted to the regional database by 3:00 PM every Friday, and I've missed the cutoff three times in the last month just because I'm staring at the screen, terrified to hit submit. And I've even started pulling back from the meetings I’m expected to attend. We have these bi-weekly departmental reviews, and I used to be the first one in the conference room, coffee in hand, ready to go over the defect trends. Now? I literally find excuses to be out on the far end of the sorting floor checking a pallet just so I don't have to sit at that table and risk him turning his attention on me. I just avoid them entirely.

And then I bring all that mess home with me, and... well, like I mentioned earlier about snapping at my husband, it's gotten to the point where we are arguing so much more than we ever used to. We've been married thirty years, and we hardly ever fought, but now? The other night he just innocently asked if I had remembered to pick up the dry cleaning—he had a couple of his good button-down shirts there, the wrinkle-free ones he likes for church—and I just completely lost it on him. I started yelling about how I have enough on my plate and how he can pick up his own shirts. It wasn't fair to him at all. 

And I'm just... I'm not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to, either. I used to have a whole system. I'd come home, unpack my lunch cooler, wipe down the kitchen counters with those Clorox wipes, maybe start a load of towels, and prep the Hamilton Beach coffee maker for the next morning so all we had to do was press a button. But now? I walk through the front door, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl in the hallway, and I just collapse. The mail just piles up on the dining room table for days, the dishes sit in the sink overnight... I just don't have the capacity for any of it once I get home. It's like all my energy is completely drained just trying to survive the shift.
Have you noticed that the stress from work has affected any other important areas of your life, like hobbies, social activities, or your overall sense of well-being?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really has bled into absolutely every corner of my life, so my overall sense of well-being is just... well, it's completely shot. 

I know I just mentioned my work record taking a hit, but I really can't emphasize enough how much that weighs on me. I mean, missing those internal deadlines? I used to be the person they used as an example during orientation for the new hires! I was the gold standard for quality assurance. And now, because I’ve pulled back from those departmental meetings I’m expected to attend, I feel like I'm letting my whole team down. I’m just hiding out on the sorting floor, avoiding eye contact, and it makes me feel terrible about myself as a professional. It really damages your self-esteem when you know you aren't performing up to your own standards.

And as for social activities or hobbies... well, that ties right back into what I was saying about my evening routines falling apart at home. Because I'm not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to, and because my husband and I are arguing so much more now, I just don't have the heart or the energy for anything fun. 

We used to have another couple from our church, the Hendersons, over for pinochle every other Friday night. It was a whole tradition. I'd bake a nice Bundt cake—usually lemon, because Frank Henderson just loves anything with lemon glaze—and we'd play cards and drink decaf until almost midnight. But I haven't invited them over in well over a month. Honestly, how can I? The mail is piled up everywhere, the dishes aren't done, and I'm so exhausted from the stress of my shift that the mere thought of entertaining just makes me want to put my head down on the table and cry. And of course, my husband gets upset because he misses seeing Frank, which just starts another argument between us about how I'm shutting people out. So yes, my social life, my marriage, my job... everything is just taking a massive hit right now, all because of what's happening at that warehouse.
Do you feel that your reaction to this manager and the changes he’s made is proportionate to the situation, or do you feel like you're responding more intensely than you expected or intended?

Oh, it is absolutely more intense than I ever intended, doctor. I mean, honestly, that's exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today. I know it's too much, but I just can't seem to stop it. 

Ever since this new operations manager showed up and just started... well, picking apart the inspection procedures I’ve used for literally years—procedures that have kept our defect rate under one percent, mind you, procedures I helped write the manual for back in 2012—I just... I can’t seem to leave work at work anymore. It used to be that I'd clock out at 3:30, walk out to the parking lot, get in my Honda, and the job stayed in the warehouse. I wouldn't give it a second thought until the next morning. 

But now? Now I come home completely wound up. My shoulders are practically up to my ears by the time I walk through the front door. And like I was saying earlier about the dry cleaning, I end up snapping at my husband over the most ridiculous, trivial things because I'm just so on edge. And then the nights... oh, the nights are just terrible. I'll get into bed, pull up the covers, and instead of just drifting off like a normal person, I just lie awake for hours. I just stare up at the ceiling fan going round and round, and I'm replaying every single thing that happened that day. I'll replay those meetings in my head, thinking, "Why did he question my sampling method on that third pallet? Did I sound defensive when I answered? Should I have brought up the calibration logs?" Just over and over and over.

And then the absolute worst part—and this is what really tells me that I'm overreacting and that this is getting out of hand—is that the very next day, I go back into the warehouse exhausted, and I actually start second-guessing the routine quality calls I used to make without a single ounce of trouble. Calls I could make in my sleep! Like, doing a visual check on a batch of components or running a simple weight variance... things I've done ten thousand times flawlessly, and suddenly I'm hesitating. I'm standing there with my clipboard, my hand shaking a little, wondering if I'm doing it wrong, wondering if he's going to come around the corner and catch me making a mistake. 

So, yes, I definitely know I'm responding way more intensely than I should be. It's completely taken over my brain, and I just don't know how to turn the worry off anymore.

Well, I don't know if I'd say they are *completely* out of my control. That makes it sound like I'm losing my mind or something, and I am definitely not doing that. I can still steer my own brain, it just takes a lot of effort right now. 

If I'm doing something that demands my absolute, undivided attention, I can push work out of my head. Like, just this past Sunday afternoon, my husband was trying to fix the carburetor on his riding mower. It’s a John Deere, we bought it secondhand about five years ago, and it's been making this awful sputtering noise whenever you engage the blades. Anyway, he has these thick fingers and he just couldn't get this tiny little retaining clip back onto the fuel line. He was getting so frustrated, his face was turning bright red, and it was already sweltering in the garage. 

So I went out there to help him, and I had to use my needle-nose pliers—the ones with the blue rubber grips that I usually keep in my craft drawer for jewelry making—and I had to get right in there at this very specific, awkward angle to snap it back into place. For those twenty minutes or so, I was so focused on not dropping that tiny little metal clip into the engine casing that I didn't think about the new operations manager or my inspection logs once. Not a single time. 

So I *can* stop thinking about work, and I can control it. It's just that... well, the second I washed the grease off my hands with the GoJo soap and sat back down in the living room with my iced tea, the worries just slipped right back in through the side door. The moment my mind isn't actively occupied by a complex task, the tape loop starts up again. But no, I wouldn't say I'm completely helpless to my own thoughts. I just have to work much, much harder to keep them at bay than I ever used to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression, particularly related to anhedonia or low mood, which could help differentiate between adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) and generalized anxiety disorder (F43.10).
doctor.question: Have you noticed any days where you feel down or low, even when things at work are going relatively okay?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling down or low (depressive symptoms) independent of the work stressor, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if things at work are actually going okay, then I feel completely fine. I'm not walking around feeling depressed or low for no reason, I promise you that. 

Like, take last Thursday for example. The new operations manager was actually out of the building for the entire day. He had some sort of regional compliance seminar down in Peoria, I think it was—one of those all-day things they hold in the conference center at the Marriott down there. Anyway, because he wasn't there pacing the floor, I went in and it was just exactly like the old days. I grabbed my clipboard, I checked the calibration on our digital scales—we use these highly sensitive Mettler Toledo scales on the line that have to be zeroed out perfectly every single morning before we can even begin—and I just went right to work. 

And doctor, I felt completely like myself. I cleared four pallets of components before my lunch break, I didn't second-guess a single defect call, and I was even humming along to the classic rock station they play over the warehouse speakers. I felt light. I wasn't down or sad whatsoever. And when I came home that evening, I actually had energy. I didn't just drop my bag and zone out on the couch like I've been doing. I actually made a proper dinner from scratch—I made my husband's favorite, chicken piccata with the capers and a nice side of angel hair pasta—and we had a lovely, normal evening together without a single argument. 

So, no, if the pressure at work isn't there and things are running the way they're supposed to, my mood is absolutely fine. I'm a very positive person by nature! It's really only when I'm dealing with him breathing down my neck and questioning my logs that I get so wound up and miserable. If work is okay, I'm okay.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to anxiety about work, which would support a diagnosis of adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) over generalized anxiety disorder (F43.10).
doctor.question: Has the way you're feeling about work affected your ability to function in any other important areas of your life, like your relationship with your husband or your ability to manage daily responsibilities at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work record has taken a hit because I’ve missed internal deadlines and pulled back from meetings I’m expected to attend. At home, my husband and I are arguing more, and I’m not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how my feelings about work have affected my functioning in other important areas of my life, such as my relationship with my husband and managing daily responsibilities, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, it absolutely has, and that's the part that really scares me, to be perfectly honest with you. Because I have always been someone who takes pride in keeping everything running smoothly, both at the warehouse and at home. 

But lately... well, my work record has actually taken a real hit, which is just devastating to me because I have had a spotless file for fifteen years. Not a single disciplinary mark. But because I'm so paralyzed by this new manager and double-checking everything I do, I’ve actually started missing our internal deadlines. We have these end-of-week quality assurance summaries that absolutely have to be submitted to the regional database by 3:00 PM every Friday, and I've missed the cutoff three times in the last month just because I'm staring at the screen, terrified to hit submit. And I've even started pulling back from the meetings I’m expected to attend. We have these bi-weekly departmental reviews, and I used to be the first one in the conference room, coffee in hand, ready to go over the defect trends. Now? I literally find excuses to be out on the far end of the sorting floor checking a pallet just so I don't have to sit at that table and risk him turning his attention on me. I just avoid them entirely.

And then I bring all that mess home with me, and... well, like I mentioned earlier about snapping at my husband, it's gotten to the point where we are arguing so much more than we ever used to. We've been married thirty years, and we hardly ever fought, but now? The other night he just innocently asked if I had remembered to pick up the dry cleaning—he had a couple of his good button-down shirts there, the wrinkle-free ones he likes for church—and I just completely lost it on him. I started yelling about how I have enough on my plate and how he can pick up his own shirts. It wasn't fair to him at all. 

And I'm just... I'm not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to, either. I used to have a whole system. I'd come home, unpack my lunch cooler, wipe down the kitchen counters with those Clorox wipes, maybe start a load of towels, and prep the Hamilton Beach coffee maker for the next morning so all we had to do was press a button. But now? I walk through the front door, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl in the hallway, and I just collapse. The mail just piles up on the dining room table for days, the dishes sit in the sink overnight... I just don't have the capacity for any of it once I get home. It's like all my energy is completely drained just trying to survive the shift.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or functional impairment in areas outside of work and home due to the stress related to the manager.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that the stress from work has affected any other important areas of your life, like hobbies, social activities, or your overall sense of well-being?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work record has taken a hit because I’ve missed internal deadlines and pulled back from meetings I’m expected to attend. At home, my husband and I are arguing more, and I’m not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how the stress has affected other areas of life such as hobbies, social activities, and overall well-being, which falls under functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really has bled into absolutely every corner of my life, so my overall sense of well-being is just... well, it's completely shot. 

I know I just mentioned my work record taking a hit, but I really can't emphasize enough how much that weighs on me. I mean, missing those internal deadlines? I used to be the person they used as an example during orientation for the new hires! I was the gold standard for quality assurance. And now, because I’ve pulled back from those departmental meetings I’m expected to attend, I feel like I'm letting my whole team down. I’m just hiding out on the sorting floor, avoiding eye contact, and it makes me feel terrible about myself as a professional. It really damages your self-esteem when you know you aren't performing up to your own standards.

And as for social activities or hobbies... well, that ties right back into what I was saying about my evening routines falling apart at home. Because I'm not keeping up with our usual evening routines the way I used to, and because my husband and I are arguing so much more now, I just don't have the heart or the energy for anything fun. 

We used to have another couple from our church, the Hendersons, over for pinochle every other Friday night. It was a whole tradition. I'd bake a nice Bundt cake—usually lemon, because Frank Henderson just loves anything with lemon glaze—and we'd play cards and drink decaf until almost midnight. But I haven't invited them over in well over a month. Honestly, how can I? The mail is piled up everywhere, the dishes aren't done, and I'm so exhausted from the stress of my shift that the mere thought of entertaining just makes me want to put my head down on the table and cry. And of course, my husband gets upset because he misses seeing Frank, which just starts another argument between us about how I'm shutting people out. So yes, my social life, my marriage, my job... everything is just taking a massive hit right now, all because of what's happening at that warehouse.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or functional impairment in direct response to the identified stressor (manager), which is key to differentiating between adjustment disorder and other anxiety disorders.
doctor.question: Do you feel that your reaction to this manager and the changes he’s made is proportionate to the situation, or do you feel like you're responding more intensely than you expected or intended?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because ever since this new operations manager started picking apart the inspection procedures I’ve used for years, I can’t seem to leave work at work—I come home wound up, snap at my husband, lie awake replaying meetings, and then the next day I second-guess routine quality calls I used to make without trouble.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the intensity and proportion of the patient's emotional and behavioral reaction to the stressor, which directly maps to the stress-related maladaptive response.

patient.answer:
Oh, it is absolutely more intense than I ever intended, doctor. I mean, honestly, that's exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today. I know it's too much, but I just can't seem to stop it. 

Ever since this new operations manager showed up and just started... well, picking apart the inspection procedures I’ve used for literally years—procedures that have kept our defect rate under one percent, mind you, procedures I helped write the manual for back in 2012—I just... I can’t seem to leave work at work anymore. It used to be that I'd clock out at 3:30, walk out to the parking lot, get in my Honda, and the job stayed in the warehouse. I wouldn't give it a second thought until the next morning. 

But now? Now I come home completely wound up. My shoulders are practically up to my ears by the time I walk through the front door. And like I was saying earlier about the dry cleaning, I end up snapping at my husband over the most ridiculous, trivial things because I'm just so on edge. And then the nights... oh, the nights are just terrible. I'll get into bed, pull up the covers, and instead of just drifting off like a normal person, I just lie awake for hours. I just stare up at the ceiling fan going round and round, and I'm replaying every single thing that happened that day. I'll replay those meetings in my head, thinking, "Why did he question my sampling method on that third pallet? Did I sound defensive when I answered? Should I have brought up the calibration logs?" Just over and over and over.

And then the absolute worst part—and this is what really tells me that I'm overreacting and that this is getting out of hand—is that the very next day, I go back into the warehouse exhausted, and I actually start second-guessing the routine quality calls I used to make without a single ounce of trouble. Calls I could make in my sleep! Like, doing a visual check on a batch of components or running a simple weight variance... things I've done ten thousand times flawlessly, and suddenly I'm hesitating. I'm standing there with my clipboard, my hand shaking a little, wondering if I'm doing it wrong, wondering if he's going to come around the corner and catch me making a mistake. 

So, yes, I definitely know I'm responding way more intensely than I should be. It's completely taken over my brain, and I just don't know how to turn the worry off anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent worry about multiple areas of life, which would support generalized anxiety disorder (F43.10), or if the worry remains limited to work-related stressors, which would support adjustment disorder (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you noticed that your worrying has started to expand beyond work, such as being more anxious about other things like your health, your finances, or things that used to not bother you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my worrying has expanded into other areas like health or finances (symptoms of Generalized Anxiety Disorder), but my symptom profile only covers my specific maladaptive response to the work stressor and its timeline/functional impairment. It does not include generalized worry about other domains.

patient.answer:
You know, doctor, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was sitting down to balance the checkbook. And the answer is really no, not at all. 

Our finances are actually in very good shape, thank goodness. We paid off the mortgage on our house—it's a lovely little three-bedroom ranch we bought back in '98—we paid that off three years ago, actually. And my husband has a solid retirement plan, and we've always been very careful savers. We've used that envelope system for budgeting for decades, you know? So I don't worry about money one bit. The bills are paid. 

And my health... well, aside from feeling completely exhausted all the time from the stress of my shifts, I don't sit around worrying that I'm coming down with some terrible disease or anything like that. I've always been very healthy. I have excellent blood pressure, my cholesterol was absolutely perfect at my last physical with my primary care doctor back in October, and I always take my multivitamin every morning with my oatmeal. So I'm not anxious about my body failing me or anything. 

So it's really not like I'm just a worrywart about everything in the world all of a sudden. Honestly, that's what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating to me! If I were just an anxious person by nature, maybe I could understand it better. But literally every single ounce of my worry, every bit of that panic that keeps me up at night staring at the ceiling fan, is one hundred percent focused on that warehouse. It's just him. It's the new operations manager, it's the quality assurance logs, it's the sampling methods... it's like my brain has this terrible laser focus on my job and it just won't shut off. I don't care about the stock market or getting sick, I just care about whether he's going to write me up for a phantom defect on line four because he doesn't like the way I filled out the clipboard. 

So, no, the worry hasn't spread to my health or my bank account or anything else. It's just completely and totally consumed the work part of my brain, and I just can't seem to pry it out of there.
